optionC: The ground rod is resonant
optionD: The ground wire has high impedance on that frequency
explanation: If the ground wire happens to have a high impedance at the operating frequency, for example because its length is near a quarter wavelength, high RF voltages appear at the equipment end and can cause RF burns. Insulated wire or braid does not cause this.

question: How does a signal that reads 20 dB over S9 compare to one that reads S9 on a receiver, assuming a properly calibrated S meter?
optionC: It is 20 times more powerful
explanation: Twenty dB is a power ratio of 10 to the power of 2, or 100, so a signal 20 dB over S9 is 100 times more powerful than one at S9. A ratio of 20 times would be only about 13 dB.

question: Which of the following most limits an HF mobile installation?
optionB: The wire gauge of the DC power line to the transceiver
optionC: Efficiency of the electrically short antenna
optionD: FCC rules limiting mobile output power on the 75-meter band
explanation: An HF mobile antenna is usually much shorter than a quarter wavelength, so it has low radiation resistance and loses much of its power in loading coils and ground losses. That inefficiency limits a mobile station far more than wire gauge does.

question: What is the purpose of an antenna tuner?
optionA: Reduce the SWR in the feed line to the antenna
optionB: Reduce the power dissipation in the feedline to the antenna
optionC: Increase power transfer from the transmitter to the feed line
explanation: An antenna tuner matches the transmitter to the impedance seen at its end of the feed line, so more power is transferred from the transmitter into the line. It does not lower the SWR or the losses on the feed line itself.

question: What is an advantage of a digital multimeter as compared to an analog multimeter?
optionC: Higher precision
explanation: A digital multimeter shows a numeric reading with more significant digits than you can read off an analog pointer, so it offers higher precision. Its response is not faster, which is why analog meters are still used for tuning.

question: What is a possible effect of a resonant ground connection?
optionC: High RF voltages on the enclosures of station equipment
explanation: A ground wire that is resonant, such as a quarter wavelength long, presents a high impedance at the station end, so high RF voltages can appear on the equipment enclosures. It does not make ground straps overheat or rods corrode.

question: How much change in signal strength is typically represented by one S unit?
optionC: 15 dB
explanation: On a calibrated S meter each S unit stands for about 6 dB, a fourfold change in power. That is why a move from S8 to S9 takes about four times the power.

question: What is one disadvantage of using a shortened mobile antenna as opposed to a full-size antenna?
optionA: Short antennas are more likely to cause distortion of transmitted signals
optionB: Q of the antenna will be very low
optionC: Operating bandwidth may be very limited
explanation: A shortened, loaded mobile antenna has a high Q, so it stays well matched over only a narrow range of frequencies and must often be retuned. Its Q is high, not very low.

question: What happens as a receiver’s noise reduction control level is increased?
optionC: CW signals may become severely attenuated
optionD: Received frequency may shift several kHz
explanation: Noise reduction (DSP) works by processing the received audio, and the harder it is set, the more it can affect the wanted signal too, so signals may sound distorted or watery. It does not shift or destabilize the frequency.

question: What signals are used to conduct a two-tone test?
optionA: Two audio signals of the same frequency shifted 90 degrees
optionC: Two swept frequency tones
optionD: Two audio frequency range square wave signals of equal amplitude
explanation: A two-tone test feeds two audio tones that are not harmonically related into an SSB transmitter. Unrelated tones make any intermodulation products easy to spot on a spectrum display and give a steady envelope to check.

question: Why should soldered joints not be used in lightning protection ground connections?
optionA: A soldered joint will likely be destroyed by the heat of a lightning strike
optionB: Solder flux will prevent a low conductivity connection
optionC: Solder has too high a dielectric constant to provide adequate lightning protection
explanation: A lightning strike carries a huge current that heats the connection, and solder melts at a low temperature, so a soldered joint will likely be destroyed. Clamped or welded connections are used instead.

question: How much must the power output of a transmitter be raised to change the S meter reading on a distant receiver from S8 to S9?
optionC: Approximately 4 times
explanation: One S unit is about 6 dB, and 6 dB is a power ratio of about 4, so the transmitter power must go up about four times to raise the reading from S8 to S9. Doubling power gives only 3 dB, half an S unit.

question: Which of the following may cause receive interference to an HF transceiver installed in a vehicle?
optionC: The control computers
explanation: All listed items are true. A vehicle's battery charging system, fuel delivery system such as the fuel pump, and control computers can all produce electrical noise that interferes with HF reception.

question: What is the correct adjustment for the LOAD or COUPLING control of a vacuum tube RF power amplifier?
optionB: Minimum plate current without exceeding maximum allowable grid current
optionC: Highest plate voltage while minimizing grid current
optionD: Desired power output without exceeding maximum allowable plate current
explanation: The LOAD or COUPLING control is set to get the desired power output without going over the tube's maximum allowable plate current. Minimum SWR at the antenna is set by the antenna system, not by this control.

question: What transmitter performance parameter does a two-tone test analyze?
optionB: Percentage of suppression of the carrier and undesired sideband for SSB
optionC: Percentage of frequency modulation
explanation: A two-tone test shows the linearity of a transmitter or amplifier: a linear one reproduces the two tones without extra intermodulation products or a flattened envelope. Carrier suppression is measured with other tests.

question: Which of the following would reduce RF interference caused by common-mode current on an audio cable?
optionA: Place a ferrite choke on the cable
optionB: Connect the center conductor to the shield of all cables to short circuit the RFI signal
optionC: Ground the center conductor of the audio cable causing the interference
optionD: Add an additional insulating jacket to the cable
explanation: A ferrite choke on the cable adds high impedance to common-mode RF current flowing on the outside of the cable, reducing the interference without affecting the audio. Shorting or grounding the center conductor would kill the audio.

question: What frequency range is occupied by a 3 kHz LSB signal when the displayed carrier frequency is set to 7.178 MHz?
optionC: 7.175 MHz to 7.178 MHz
explanation: Lower sideband sits below the displayed carrier frequency, so a 3 kHz LSB signal set at 7.178 MHz occupies 7.175 to 7.178 MHz. The range 7.178 to 7.181 MHz would be upper sideband.

question: In what configuration are the individual cells in a solar panel connected together?
optionC: Bypass
explanation: Solar cells are wired in series to build up voltage and in parallel to build up current, so a panel uses a series-parallel arrangement. Shunt and bypass are not ways of combining the cells.

question: What is the purpose of delaying RF output after activating a transmitter’s keying line to an external amplifier?
optionA: To prevent key clicks on CW
optionC: To allow time for the amplifier to switch the antenna between the transceiver and the amplifier output
optionD: To allow time for the amplifier power supply to reach operating level
explanation: The external amplifier needs a few milliseconds after keying to switch its relays and connect the antenna to its output; delaying RF avoids sending power into open or switching contacts. It is not about key clicks.

question: When is an analog multimeter preferred to a digital multimeter?
optionC: When measuring the frequency of an oscillator
optionD: When adjusting circuits for maximum or minimum values
explanation: An analog meter's moving pointer makes it easy to see a peak or dip while adjusting a circuit for maximum or minimum, where a digital display's changing digits are hard to follow. Digital meters are better for precision.

question: How can the effects of ground loops be minimized?
optionA: Connect all ground conductors in series
optionB: Connect the AC neutral conductor to the ground wire
optionC: Avoid using lock washers and star washers when making ground connections
explanation: Bonding all equipment enclosures together with short, heavy conductors keeps them at the same potential, so less current flows between them through cable shields and ground loops are minimized. Connecting grounds in series makes things worse.

question: What frequency range is occupied by a 3 kHz USB signal with the displayed carrier frequency set to 14.347 MHz?
optionC: 14.344 MHz to 14.347 MHz
explanation: Upper sideband sits above the displayed carrier frequency, so a 3 kHz USB signal set at 14.347 MHz occupies 14.347 to 14.350 MHz. The range 14.344 to 14.347 MHz would be lower sideband.

question: What is the approximate open-circuit voltage from a fully illuminated silicon photovoltaic cell?
optionC: 0.2 VDC
explanation: A fully lit silicon photovoltaic cell gives about 0.5 volts with no load, which is why many cells are connected in series to reach a useful voltage. A figure of 1.38 volts is far too high for one silicon cell.

question: What is the function of an electronic keyer?
optionB: Automatic generation of dots and dashes for CW operation
optionC: To allow time for switching the antenna from the receiver to the transmitter
optionD: Computer interface for PSK and RTTY operation
explanation: An electronic keyer automatically forms dots and dashes of correct length and spacing from a paddle, making CW sending easier and more even. Transmit and receive switching is done by other circuits.

question: Which of the following can be determined with a directional wattmeter?
optionC: RF interference
explanation: A directional wattmeter measures forward and reflected power separately, and from those two readings you can work out the standing wave ratio. It cannot tell you an antenna's front-to-back ratio or propagation.

question: What could be a symptom caused by a ground loop in your station’s audio connections?
optionA: You receive reports of “hum” on your station’s transmitted signal
optionB: The SWR reading for one or more antennas is suddenly very high
optionC: An item of station equipment starts to draw excessive amounts of current
optionD: You receive reports of harmonic interference from your station
explanation: A ground loop in audio connections lets AC-related current flow in cable shields, which adds hum to the audio and therefore to your transmitted signal. It does not change the antenna SWR.

question: How close to the lower edge of a band’s phone segment should your displayed carrier frequency be when using 3 kHz wide LSB?
optionA: At least 3 kHz above the edge of the segment
optionB: At least 3 kHz below the edge of the segment
optionC: At least 1 kHz below the edge of the segment
optionD: At least 1 kHz above the edge of the segment
explanation: LSB extends about 3 kHz below the displayed carrier frequency, so the carrier must be at least 3 kHz above the lower edge of the phone segment to keep the whole signal inside it. A 1 kHz margin would let 2 kHz spill out.

question: Why should a series diode be connected between a solar panel and a storage battery that is being charged by the panel?
optionA: To prevent overload by regulating the charging voltage
optionB: To prevent discharge of the battery through the panel during times of low or no illumination
optionC: To limit the current flowing from the panel to a safe value
optionD: To prevent damage to the battery due to excessive voltage at high illumination levels
explanation: When the panel is dark its output voltage drops below the battery's, and current could flow back from the battery through the panel. A series diode blocks that reverse flow. It does not regulate the charging voltage.

question: Why should the ALC system be inactive when transmitting AFSK data signals?
optionA: ALC will invert the modulation of the AFSK mode
optionB: The ALC action distorts the signal
optionC: When using digital modes, too much ALC activity can cause the transmitter to overheat
explanation: AFSK data modes need a clean, linear signal, and ALC action changes the gain unevenly and distorts it, causing splatter and errors. Drive is set by audio level so ALC stays inactive; ALC does not invert the modulation.

question: Which of the following must be connected to an antenna analyzer when it is being used for SWR measurements?
optionC: Antenna and feed line
explanation: An antenna analyzer contains its own low-power signal source, so for an SWR check you connect it to the antenna and its feed line. Neither the transmitter nor a receiver is connected.

question: What technique helps to minimize RF “hot spots” in an amateur station?
optionA: Building all equipment in a metal enclosure
optionC: Bonding all equipment enclosures together
optionD: Placing low-pass filters on all feed lines
explanation: Bonding all equipment enclosures together keeps them at one RF potential, so there are fewer points where RF voltage builds up and causes hot spots. Surge suppressor outlets protect against power surges, not RF.

question: How close to the upper edge of a band’s phone segment should your displayed carrier frequency be when using 3 kHz wide USB?
optionA: At least 3 kHz above the edge of the band
optionB: At least 3 kHz below the edge of the band
optionC: At least 1 kHz above the edge of the segment
optionD: At least 1 kHz below the edge of the segment
explanation: USB extends about 3 kHz above the displayed carrier frequency, so the carrier must be at least 3 kHz below the upper edge of the band to keep the whole signal inside it. Setting it above the edge would put you out of band.

question: What precaution should be taken when connecting a solar panel to a lithium iron phosphate battery?
optionA: Ground the solar panel outer metal framework
optionB: Ensure the battery is placed terminals-up
optionC: A series resistor must be in place
optionD: The solar panel must have a charge controller
explanation: Lithium iron phosphate batteries need carefully controlled charging voltage and current, so a charge controller suited to that chemistry must sit between the solar panel and the battery. A series resistor cannot do this job.

question: Which of the following is a common use of the dual-VFO feature on a transceiver?
optionA: To allow transmitting on two frequencies at once
optionB: To permit full duplex operation -- that is, transmitting and receiving at the same time
optionC: To transmit on one frequency and listen on another
optionD: To improve frequency accuracy by allowing variable frequency output (VFO) operation
explanation: Dual VFOs let you transmit on one frequency and listen on another, which is how split operation works, for example with DX stations. They do not let you transmit on two frequencies or work full duplex.

question: What effect can strong signals from nearby transmitters have on an antenna analyzer?
optionA: Desensitization which can cause intermodulation products which interfere with impedance readings
optionB: Received power that interferes with SWR readings
optionC: Generation of harmonics which interfere with frequency readings
explanation: An antenna analyzer works with very low power, so strong signals picked up from nearby transmitters add received power at its input and throw off its SWR readings. It does not generate harmonics from them.

question: Why must all metal enclosures of station equipment be grounded?
optionA: It prevents a blown fuse in the event of an internal short circuit
optionC: It ensures that the neutral wire is grounded
optionD: It ensures that hazardous voltages cannot appear on the chassis
explanation: Grounding a metal enclosure means that if a live wire touches it, the current flows to ground and trips a breaker or fuse instead of leaving a dangerous voltage on the chassis. It does not prevent a fuse from blowing.

question: What is the purpose of using a receive attenuator?
optionA: To prevent receiver overload from strong incoming signals
optionB: To reduce the transmitter power when driving a linear amplifier
optionC: To reduce power consumption when operating from batteries
optionD: To reduce excessive audio level on strong signals
explanation: A receive attenuator lowers incoming signal levels before the receiver front end, preventing overload when very strong signals are present. It has no effect on transmit power or on audio volume.

question: Which of the following can be measured with an antenna analyzer?
optionC: Impedance of coaxial cable
explanation: An antenna analyzer measures impedance, SWR and related values at its connector, so it can measure the impedance of coaxial cable, for example characteristic impedance with the far end terminated. It cannot measure antenna gain or transmitter output.

question: What happens when inductive and capacitive reactance are equal in a series LC circuit?
optionA: Resonance causes impedance to be very high
optionB: Impedance is equal to the geometric mean of the inductance and capacitance
optionC: Resonance causes impedance to be very low
optionD: Impedance is equal to the arithmetic mean of the inductance and capacitance
explanation: At series resonance the inductive and capacitive reactances cancel, leaving only the circuit's resistance, so impedance falls to a minimum. Very high impedance at resonance describes a parallel LC circuit, not a series one.

question: What dB change represents a factor of two increase or decrease in power?
optionC: Approximately 6 dB
explanation: A doubling or halving of power is 10 log(2) = about 3 dB. 6 dB is a factor of four in power, or of two in voltage.

question: What causes a voltage to appear across the secondary winding of a transformer when an AC voltage source is connected across its primary winding?
optionC: Mutual inductance
explanation: The changing magnetic field from the primary current links the secondary winding and induces a voltage in it. This coupling between two coils is mutual inductance.

question: What is reactance?
optionA: Opposition to the flow of direct current caused by resistance
optionB: Opposition to the flow of alternating current caused by capacitance or inductance
optionC: Reinforcement of the flow of direct current caused by resistance
optionD: Reinforcement of the flow of alternating current caused by capacitance or inductance
explanation: Reactance is the opposition that capacitors and inductors present to alternating current. Unlike resistance, it stores energy rather than dissipating it, and it changes with frequency.

question: How does the total current relate to the individual currents in a circuit of parallel resistors?
optionA: It equals the average of the branch currents
optionB: It decreases as more parallel branches are added to the circuit
optionC: It equals the sum of the currents through each branch
optionD: It is the sum of the reciprocal of each individual voltage drop
explanation: In a parallel circuit every branch has the same voltage, and the total current is the sum of the branch currents (Kirchhoff's current law). Adding branches increases total current, not decreases it.

question: What is the output voltage if an input signal is applied to the secondary winding of a 4:1 voltage step-down transformer instead of the primary winding?
optionA: The input voltage is multiplied by 4
optionB: The input voltage is divided by 4
optionC: Additional resistance must be added in series with the primary to prevent overload
optionD: Additional resistance must be added in parallel with the secondary to prevent overload
explanation: A transformer works in both directions. Feeding a 4:1 step-down transformer from its secondary makes it a 1:4 step-up transformer, so the input voltage is multiplied by 4.

question: Which of the following is opposition to the flow of alternating current in an inductor?
optionC: Admittance
explanation: An inductor opposes AC through inductive reactance, XL = 2 pi f L. Reluctance sounds plausible but is opposition to magnetic flux in a magnetic circuit, not to current.

question: How many watts of electrical power are consumed if 400 VDC is supplied to an 800-ohm load?
optionC: 400 watts
explanation: P = E squared / R = 400 x 400 / 800 = 200 watts.

question: What is the total resistance of a 10-, a 20-, and a 50-ohm resistor connected in parallel?
optionC: 17 ohms
explanation: 1/R = 1/10 + 1/20 + 1/50 = 0.1 + 0.05 + 0.02 = 0.17, so R = 1/0.17 = about 5.9 ohms. Parallel resistance is always less than the smallest resistor.

question: Which of the following is opposition to the flow of alternating current in a capacitor?
optionC: Reactance
explanation: A capacitor opposes AC through capacitive reactance, XC = 1/(2 pi f C). Conductance and admittance measure how easily current flows, the opposite idea.

question: How many watts of electrical power are consumed by a 12 VDC light bulb that draws 0.2 amperes?
optionC: 6 watts
explanation: P = E x I = 12 V x 0.2 A = 2.4 watts.

question: What is the approximate total resistance of a 100- and a 200-ohm resistor in parallel?
optionC: 75 ohms

question: How does an inductor react to AC?
optionA: As the frequency of the applied AC increases, the reactance decreases
optionB: As the amplitude of the applied AC increases, the reactance increases
optionC: As the amplitude of the applied AC increases, the reactance decreases
optionD: As the frequency of the applied AC increases, the reactance increases
explanation: Inductive reactance is XL = 2 pi f L, so it rises in direct proportion to frequency. The amplitude of the AC has no effect on reactance.

question: How many watts are consumed when a current of 7.0 milliamperes flows through a 1,250-ohm resistance?
optionC: Approximately 11 milliwatts
explanation: P = I squared x R = (0.007 A) squared x 1,250 ohms = 0.06125 W, about 61 milliwatts.

question: Why is the primary winding wire of a voltage step-up transformer usually a larger size than that of the secondary winding?
optionA: To improve the coupling between the primary and secondary
optionB: To accommodate the higher current of the primary
optionC: To prevent parasitic oscillations due to resistive losses in the primary
optionD: To ensure that the volume of the primary winding is equal to the volume of the secondary winding
explanation: Power in equals power out, so the side with lower voltage carries more current. In a step-up transformer that is the primary, which needs heavier wire.

question: How does a capacitor react to AC?
optionA: As the frequency of the applied AC increases, the reactance decreases
optionB: As the frequency of the applied AC increases, the reactance increases
optionC: As the amplitude of the applied AC increases, the reactance increases
optionD: As the amplitude of the applied AC increases, the reactance decreases
explanation: Capacitive reactance is XC = 1/(2 pi f C), so it falls as frequency rises. Amplitude does not change reactance.

question: What is the PEP produced by 200 volts peak-to-peak across a 50-ohm dummy load?
optionC: 353.5 watts
explanation: 200 V peak-to-peak is 100 V peak, and 100 x 0.707 = 70.7 V RMS. PEP = E squared / R = 70.7 x 70.7 / 50 = 100 watts.

question: What is the voltage output of a transformer with a 500-turn primary and a 1500-turn secondary when 120 VAC is applied to the primary?
optionC: 40 volts
explanation: Output voltage scales with the turns ratio: 120 V x (1500 / 500) = 120 x 3 = 360 volts.

question: What is the term for the inverse of impedance?
optionC: Reluctance
explanation: Admittance (Y) is the reciprocal of impedance, Y = 1/Z, measured in siemens. Conductance is only the inverse of resistance, and susceptance only the inverse of reactance.

question: What value of an AC signal produces the same power dissipation in a resistor as a DC voltage of the same value?
optionC: The RMS value
optionD: The reciprocal of the RMS value
explanation: The RMS (root mean square) value of an AC signal is defined as the DC voltage that would heat a resistor equally. Peak and peak-to-peak values are larger than the effective value.

question: What transformer turns ratio matches an antenna’s 600-ohm feed point impedance to a 50-ohm coaxial cable?
optionC: 24 to 1
explanation: Turns ratio = square root of the impedance ratio = square root of (600 / 50) = square root of 12 = about 3.5 to 1. 12 to 1 is the impedance ratio, not the turns ratio.

question: What is impedance?
optionA: The ratio of current to voltage
optionB: The product of current and voltage
optionC: The ratio of voltage to current
optionD: The product of current and reactance
explanation: Impedance is the ratio of voltage to current, Z = E/I, Ohm's law extended to AC circuits. The ratio of current to voltage is admittance, its inverse.

question: What is the peak-to-peak voltage of a sine wave with an RMS voltage of 120 volts?
optionC: 240.0 volts
explanation: Peak = 120 x 1.414 = 169.7 V, and peak-to-peak is twice that: 2 x 169.7 = 339.4 volts. 169.7 V is only the peak value.

question: What is the equivalent capacitance of two 5.0-nanofarad capacitors and one 750-picofarad capacitor connected in parallel?
optionC: 3,583 picofarads
explanation: Parallel capacitances add: 5.0 nF + 5.0 nF + 0.75 nF (750 pF) = 10.75 nanofarads.

question: What unit is used to measure reactance?
optionC: Ampere
explanation: Reactance is opposition to current, so like resistance and impedance it is measured in ohms. The siemens is the unit for the inverses: conductance, susceptance and admittance.

question: What is the RMS voltage of a sine wave with a value of 17 volts peak?
optionC: 24 volts
explanation: RMS = peak x 0.707 = 17 x 0.707 = about 12 volts.

question: What is the capacitance of three 100-microfarad capacitors connected in series?
optionC: 33.3 microfarads
explanation: Equal capacitors in series give the value of one divided by how many there are: 100 microfarads / 3 = 33.3 microfarads.

question: Which of the following devices can be used for impedance matching at radio frequencies?
optionC: A length of transmission line
explanation: All listed items are true: a transformer, a Pi-network and a suitable length of transmission line (such as a quarter-wave section) can each transform one impedance to another at RF.

question: What percentage of power loss is equivalent to a loss of 1 dB?
optionC: 20.6 percent
explanation: A 1 dB loss leaves 10^(-0.1) = 0.794 of the power, so the loss is 1 - 0.794 = 0.206, about 20.6 percent.

question: What is the inductance of three 10-millihenry inductors connected in parallel?
optionC: 3.3 millihenries
explanation: Equal inductors in parallel give the value of one divided by how many there are: 10 mH / 3 = 3.3 millihenries.

question: What letter is used to represent reactance?
optionC: B
explanation: Reactance uses the symbol X, as in XL and XC. Z is impedance, B is susceptance and Y is admittance.

question: What is the ratio of PEP to average power for an unmodulated carrier?
explanation: An unmodulated carrier has a constant envelope, so its peak envelope power equals its average power, a ratio of 1.00.

question: What is the inductance of a circuit with a 20-millihenry inductor connected in series with a 50-millihenry inductor?
optionC: 70 millihenries
explanation: Series inductances add like series resistors: 20 mH + 50 mH = 70 millihenries.

question: What occurs in an LC circuit at resonance?
optionC: The circuit radiates all its energy in the form of radio waves
optionD: Inductive reactance and capacitive reactance cancel
explanation: At resonance XL equals XC, and because they are opposite in phase they cancel, leaving only resistance. Resistance itself is not cancelled.

question: What is the RMS voltage across a 50-ohm dummy load dissipating 1200 watts?
optionC: 346 volts
explanation: E = square root of (P x R) = square root of (1200 x 50) = square root of 60,000 = about 245 volts RMS.

question: What is the capacitance of a 20-microfarad capacitor connected in series with a 50-microfarad capacitor?
optionC: 70 microfarads
explanation: Series capacitors combine like parallel resistors: C = (20 x 50) / (20 + 50) = 1000 / 70 = about 14.3 microfarads.

question: What is the output PEP of an unmodulated carrier if the average power is 1060 watts?
optionC: 1500 watts
explanation: An unmodulated carrier's envelope never varies, so PEP equals average power: 1060 watts.

question: Which of the following components should be added to a capacitor to increase the capacitance?
optionC: A capacitor in parallel
explanation: Capacitances in parallel add, so a capacitor in parallel raises the total. A capacitor in series lowers the total capacitance.

question: What is the output PEP of 500 volts peak-to-peak across a 50-ohm load?
optionC: 2500 watts
explanation: 500 V peak-to-peak is 250 V peak, and 250 x 0.707 = 176.8 V RMS. PEP = 176.8 x 176.8 / 50 = about 625 watts.

question: Which of the following components should be added to an inductor to increase the inductance?
optionC: An inductor in parallel
explanation: Inductances in series add, so an inductor in series raises the total. An inductor in parallel lowers it.

question: What is the minimum allowable discharge voltage for maximum life of a standard 12-volt lead-acid battery?
optionC: 10.5 volts
explanation: Discharging a 12-volt lead-acid battery below about 10.5 volts damages the plates and shortens its life. Going down to 8.5 or 6 volts would be a deep discharge that harms the battery.

question: What determines the performance of a ferrite core at different frequencies?
optionC: The composition, or “mix,” of materials used
optionD: The ratio of outer diameter to inner diameter
explanation: A ferrite core's behavior at different frequencies depends on its composition, called the mix. Different mixes are chosen for different frequency ranges.

question: What is an advantage of batteries with low internal resistance?
optionC: High voltage
explanation: Low internal resistance means little voltage is lost inside the battery under load, so it can deliver high current. That suits loads like transceivers on transmit.

question: What is meant by the term MMIC?
optionC: Metal Monolayer Integrated Circuit
explanation: MMIC stands for Monolithic Microwave Integrated Circuit, a small IC amplifier or other block made for VHF, UHF and microwave work.

question: What is the approximate forward threshold voltage of a germanium diode?
optionC: 0.7 volts
explanation: A germanium diode begins to conduct at about 0.3 volts forward bias, lower than the roughly 0.7 volts of a silicon diode.

question: Which of the following is an advantage of CMOS integrated circuits compared to TTL integrated circuits?
optionC: Better suited for RF amplification
optionD: Better suited for power supply regulation
explanation: CMOS logic draws very little current except when switching, so it uses far less power than TTL.

question: Which of the following is characteristic of an electrolytic capacitor?
optionB: Much less leakage than any other type
optionC: High capacitance for a given volume
explanation: Electrolytic capacitors pack a large capacitance into a small volume, which is why they are used as power supply filters. They have loose tolerances and relatively high leakage.

question: What is a typical upper frequency limit for low SWR operation of 50-ohm BNC connectors?
optionC: 4 GHz
explanation: A 50-ohm BNC connector keeps a low SWR up to about 4 GHz. Above that its performance falls off.

question: What is the approximate forward threshold voltage of a silicon junction diode?
optionC: 0.7 volts
explanation: A silicon junction diode starts to conduct at about 0.7 volts forward bias. About 0.3 volts is the figure for germanium.

question: What is an advantage of using a ferrite core toroidal inductor?
optionA: Large values of inductance may be obtained
optionB: The magnetic properties of the core may be optimized for a specific range of frequencies
optionC: Most of the magnetic field is contained in the core
explanation: All listed items are true: a ferrite toroid gives large inductance with few turns, its core mix can be chosen for a frequency range, and its closed shape keeps most of the magnetic field inside the core.

question: Why should wire-wound resistors not be used in RF circuits?
optionA: The resistor’s tolerance value would not be adequate
optionB: The resistor’s inductance could make circuit performance unpredictable
optionC: The resistor could overheat
optionD: The resistor’s internal capacitance would detune the circuit
explanation: A wire-wound resistor is a coil of wire, so it has inductance. At RF that inductance adds reactance and makes circuit behavior unpredictable.

question: What kind of device is an integrated circuit operational amplifier?
optionC: Programmable Logic
explanation: An op-amp is an analog device: it amplifies continuously varying signals rather than handling digital on/off levels.

question: What are the operating points for a bipolar transistor used as a switch?
optionB: The active region (between cutoff and saturation)
optionC: Peak and valley current points
explanation: A transistor switch is driven either fully on (saturation) or fully off (cutoff). The active region in between is used for linear amplification.

question: Which of the following describes a type N connector?
optionA: A moisture-resistant RF connector useful to 10 GHz
optionB: A small bayonet connector used for data circuits
optionC: A low noise figure VHF connector
optionD: A nickel plated version of the PL-259
explanation: The type N connector is a threaded, weather-resistant RF connector that works well up to about 10 GHz, making it popular for VHF, UHF and microwave feed lines.

question: Which of the following is characteristic of low voltage ceramic capacitors?
optionC: High capacitance for given volume
explanation: Low voltage ceramic capacitors are cheap and widely used for bypassing. Their tolerance and stability are generally not as good as other types.

question: How is an LED biased when emitting light?
optionC: Reverse biased
explanation: An LED emits light when it is forward biased and current flows through the junction. Reverse biased, it does not conduct and gives no light.

question: Which of the following describes MOSFET construction?
optionA: The gate is formed by a back-biased junction
optionB: The gate is separated from the channel by a thin insulating layer
optionC: The source is separated from the drain by a thin insulating layer
optionD: The source is formed by depositing metal on silicon
explanation: In a MOSFET the gate is a metal (or polysilicon) electrode insulated from the channel by a thin oxide layer, which gives it a very high input impedance. A back-biased junction gate describes a JFET.

question: How does a ferrite bead or core reduce common-mode RF current on the shield of a coaxial cable?
optionA: By creating an impedance in the current’s path
optionB: It converts common-mode current to differential mode current
optionC: By creating an out-of-phase current to cancel the common-mode current
explanation: A ferrite bead or core around the coax adds impedance to current flowing on the outside of the shield, which reduces that common-mode current. It does not convert or cancel the current.

question: Which element of a vacuum tube regulates the flow of electrons between cathode and plate?
optionC: Screen grid
explanation: The control grid, between cathode and plate, sets how many electrons reach the plate; a small voltage on it controls a large plate current. The screen and suppressor grids serve other purposes.

question: What is an SMA connector?
optionB: A small threaded connector suitable for signals up to several GHz
optionC: A connector designed for serial multiple access signals
optionD: A type of push-on connector intended for high-voltage applications
explanation: SMA (SubMiniature version A) is a small threaded coaxial connector that works to several gigahertz, common on handheld radios and microwave gear.

question: What happens when an inductor is operated above its self-resonant frequency?
optionC: It becomes capacitive
explanation: Above its self-resonant frequency, the capacitance between an inductor's turns dominates, so the component acts like a capacitor rather than an inductor.

question: Which of these connector types is commonly used for low frequency or dc signal connections to a transceiver?
optionC: RCA Phono
explanation: RCA phono connectors are cheap and common for audio, low frequency and DC connections such as accessory jacks. PL-259, BNC and type N are RF connectors.

question: What is the primary purpose of a screen grid in a vacuum tube?
optionC: To increase the control grid resistance
explanation: The screen grid sits between the control grid and the plate and shields them from each other, reducing grid-to-plate capacitance. That helps prevent unwanted oscillation.

question: What is the function of a power supply bleeder resistor?
optionA: It acts as a fuse for excess voltage
optionB: It discharges the filter capacitors when power is removed
optionC: It removes shock hazards from the induction coils
explanation: A bleeder resistor across the filter capacitors drains their stored charge after power is removed, so the supply is safe to work on. It is not a fuse.

question: What is the purpose of neutralizing an amplifier?
optionC: To cut off the final amplifier during standby periods
optionD: To keep the carrier on frequency
explanation: Neutralizing feeds back a signal that cancels the unwanted feedback through the amplifying device's internal capacitance, which eliminates self-oscillation.

question: What circuit is used to select one of the sidebands from a balanced modulator?
optionC: IF amplifier
explanation: A balanced modulator produces both sidebands with the carrier suppressed; a sharp filter then passes one sideband and rejects the other to make SSB.

question: Which of the following components are used in a power supply filter network?
optionC: Capacitors and inductors
explanation: Capacitors and inductors smooth the pulsating DC from the rectifier: capacitors hold up the voltage and inductors oppose changes in current. Diodes rectify, they do not filter.

question: Which of these classes of amplifiers has the highest efficiency?
optionC: Class AB
explanation: A Class C amplifier conducts for less than half the cycle, so it wastes the least power and is the most efficient, though it is not linear.

question: What output is produced by a balanced modulator?
optionC: Audio extracted from the modulation signal
explanation: A balanced modulator cancels the carrier and outputs both sidebands, called double-sideband suppressed-carrier RF.

question: Which type of rectifier circuit uses two diodes and a center-tapped transformer?
optionC: Half-wave
explanation: A full-wave center-tap rectifier uses two diodes, each conducting on alternate half cycles from opposite ends of a center-tapped winding. A full-wave bridge uses four diodes and needs no center tap.

question: Which of the following describes the function of a two-input AND gate?
optionA: Output is high when either or both inputs are low
optionB: Output is high only when both inputs are high
optionC: Output is low when either or both inputs are high
optionD: Output is low only when both inputs are high
explanation: A two-input AND gate gives a high output only when both inputs are high; any low input makes the output low.

question: What is one reason to use an impedance matching transformer at a transmitter output?
optionB: To present the desired impedance to the transmitter and feed line
optionC: To reduce power supply ripple
explanation: A matching transformer converts the feed line or load impedance to the impedance the transmitter is designed for, so power transfers efficiently.

question: What is characteristic of a half-wave rectifier in a power supply?
optionB: The ripple frequency is twice that of a full-wave rectifier
optionC: More current can be drawn from the half-wave rectifier
optionD: The output voltage is two times the peak input voltage
explanation: A half-wave rectifier needs only one diode. Its ripple frequency equals the AC frequency, half that of a full-wave rectifier.

question: In a Class A amplifier, what percentage of the time does the amplifying device conduct?
explanation: A Class A amplifier conducts for the whole cycle, 100 percent of the time, which makes it very linear but inefficient.

question: How is a product detector used?
optionA: Used in test gear to detect spurious mixing products
optionB: Used in a transmitter to perform frequency multiplication
optionC: Used in an FM receiver to filter out unwanted sidebands
optionD: Used in a single sideband receiver to extract the modulated signal
explanation: A product detector mixes the incoming SSB (or CW) signal with a locally generated carrier to recover the audio in a single sideband receiver.

question: What portion of the AC cycle is converted to DC by a half-wave rectifier?
optionC: 270 degrees
explanation: A half-wave rectifier conducts only on one half of each cycle, so 180 degrees of the 360-degree cycle is converted to DC.

question: How many states does a 3-bit binary counter have?
explanation: A 3-bit counter has 2 x 2 x 2 = 2^3 = 8 states, counting 0 through 7.

question: Which of the following is characteristic of a direct digital synthesizer (DDS)?
optionC: Pure sine wave output
optionD: Variable output frequency with the stability of a crystal oscillator
explanation: A DDS creates its output digitally from a crystal-controlled clock, so its frequency can be changed in fine steps while keeping crystal stability. Its output is not perfectly pure.

question: What portion of the AC cycle is converted to DC by a full-wave rectifier?
optionC: 270 degrees
explanation: A full-wave rectifier uses both halves of the cycle, so all 360 degrees is converted to DC.

question: What is a shift register?
optionA: A clocked array of circuits that passes data in steps along the array
optionB: An array of operational amplifiers used for tri-state arithmetic operations
optionC: A digital mixer
explanation: A shift register is a clocked chain of flip-flops; on each clock pulse the stored data moves one step along the chain.

question: Which of the following is an advantage of a digital signal processing (DSP) filter compared to an analog filter?
optionA: A wide range of filter bandwidths and shapes can be created
optionC: Mixing products are greatly reduced
optionD: The DSP filter is much more effective at VHF frequencies
explanation: DSP filters are defined in software, so a wide range of bandwidths and shapes can be created and changed easily, which is hard with fixed analog components.

question: What is the output waveform of an unfiltered full-wave rectifier connected to a resistive load?
optionA: A series of DC pulses at twice the frequency of the AC input
optionB: A series of DC pulses at the same frequency as the AC input
optionC: A sine wave at half the frequency of the AC input
explanation: A full-wave rectifier turns each half cycle into a positive pulse, so the output is DC pulses at twice the input frequency (120 pulses a second from 60 Hz).

question: Which of the following are basic components of a sine wave oscillator?
optionB: A frequency multiplier and a mixer
optionC: A circulator and a filter operating in a feed-forward loop
optionD: A filter and an amplifier operating in a feedback loop
explanation: A sine wave oscillator needs an amplifier and a frequency-selective filter, with the filter's output fed back to the amplifier's input in phase to sustain oscillation.

question: What term specifies a filter’s attenuation inside its passband?
optionC: Q
explanation: Insertion loss is how much a filter attenuates signals inside its passband. Ultimate rejection is how well it blocks signals outside the passband.

question: Which of the following is characteristic of a switchmode power supply as compared to a linear power supply?
optionA: Faster switching time makes higher output voltage possible
optionC: High-frequency operation allows the use of smaller components
explanation: A switchmode supply runs at high frequency, so its transformers and filter components can be much smaller and lighter than those of a linear supply.

question: How is the efficiency of an RF power amplifier determined?
optionA: Divide the DC input power by the DC output power
optionB: Divide the RF output power by the DC input power
optionC: Multiply the RF input power by the reciprocal of the RF output power
optionD: Add the RF input power to the DC output power
explanation: Efficiency = RF output power / DC input power. For example, 600 W out from 1000 W of DC input is 60 percent efficient.

question: Which parameter affects receiver sensitivity?
optionC: Input amplifier noise figure
explanation: All listed items are true: input amplifier gain, demodulator bandwidth and input amplifier noise figure all affect how weak a signal a receiver can detect.

question: What determines the frequency of an LC oscillator?
optionA: The number of stages in the counter
optionB: The number of stages in the divider
optionC: The inductance and capacitance in the tank circuit
optionD: The time delay of the lag circuit
explanation: An LC oscillator runs at the resonant frequency of its tank circuit, f = 1/(2 pi times the square root of LC), so the inductance and capacitance set the frequency.

question: What is the phase difference between the I and Q RF signals that software-defined radio (SDR) equipment uses for modulation and demodulation?
optionC: 180 degrees
explanation: The I (in-phase) and Q (quadrature) signals are 90 degrees apart, which lets an SDR represent both amplitude and phase of a signal.

question: Which of the following describes a linear amplifier?
optionA: Any RF power amplifier used in conjunction with an amateur transceiver
optionB: An amplifier in which the output preserves the input waveform
optionC: A Class C high efficiency amplifier
optionD: An amplifier used as a frequency multiplier
explanation: A linear amplifier produces an output that is a faithful, larger copy of its input waveform, which is needed for modes like SSB. Class C is not linear.

question: What is an advantage of using I-Q modulation with software-defined radios (SDRs)?
optionA: The need for high resolution analog-to-digital converters is eliminated
optionB: All types of modulation can be created with appropriate processing
optionC: Minimum detectible signal level is reduced
optionD: Automatic conversion of the signal from digital to analog
explanation: With I and Q signals, software can produce any combination of amplitude and phase, so all types of modulation can be created with the right processing.

question: For which of the following modes is a Class C power stage appropriate for amplifying a modulated signal?
optionC: AM
explanation: FM carries information only in frequency, with constant amplitude, so a nonlinear Class C stage can amplify it without distortion. SSB and AM need a linear amplifier.

question: Which of these functions is performed by software in a software-defined radio (SDR)?
optionC: Modulation
explanation: All listed items are true: in an SDR, filtering, detection and modulation are done by software operating on the digitized signal.

question: What is the frequency above which a low-pass filter’s output power is less than half the input power?
optionC: Cutoff frequency
explanation: The cutoff frequency is where output power falls to half the input, the 3 dB point; above it a low-pass filter attenuates more.

question: What term specifies a filter’s maximum ability to reject signals outside its passband?
optionC: Insertion loss
explanation: Ultimate rejection is the most attenuation a filter can give signals well outside its passband. Insertion loss is the loss inside the passband.

question: The bandwidth of a band-pass filter is measured between what two frequencies?
optionC: Pole and zero
explanation: A band-pass filter's bandwidth is measured between its upper and lower half-power (3 dB down) frequencies.

question: How is direct binary FSK modulation generated?
optionA: By keying an FM transmitter with a sub-audible tone
optionB: By changing an oscillator’s frequency directly with a digital control signal
optionC: By using a transceiver’s computer data interface protocol to change frequencies
optionD: By reconfiguring the CW keying input to act as a tone generator
explanation: Direct FSK shifts the oscillator itself between two frequencies under control of the digital data line. Keying a CW input or sending audio tones into an SSB transmitter makes AFSK or tones, not direct FSK.

question: Which mixer input is varied or tuned to convert signals of different frequencies to an intermediate frequency (IF)?
optionC: RF input
explanation: In a superhet the local oscillator is tuned so that it mixes with each desired RF signal to land on the fixed IF. The RF input is the incoming signal, not the input you tune.

question: Which digital mode is used as a low-power beacon for assessing HF propagation?
optionC: PSK31
explanation: WSPR (Weak Signal Propagation Reporter) stations send low-power beacon transmissions that are decoded and reported online, showing where a band is open. PSK31 is a keyboard chat mode, not a beacon system.

question: What is the name of the process that changes the phase angle of an RF signal to convey information?
optionC: Phase transformation
explanation: Phase modulation conveys information by shifting the phase angle of the RF carrier. Phase inversion is just a 180 degree flip, not the name of the modulation process.

question: What is the term for interference from a signal at twice the IF frequency from the desired signal?
optionC: Mixer interference
explanation: Image response is reception of a signal on the other side of the local oscillator, 2 x IF away from the wanted signal, which also mixes down to the IF. Front-end filtering and a high IF reduce it.

question: What part of a packet radio frame contains the routing and handling information?
optionC: Header
explanation: The header of a packet frame carries the routing and handling information, such as the source and destination callsigns and digipeater path. The data payload follows it.

question: What is the name of the process that changes the instantaneous frequency of an RF wave to convey information?
optionC: Frequency conversion
explanation: Frequency modulation varies the carrier's instantaneous frequency in step with the information. Frequency conversion only moves a signal to another frequency, as a mixer does, without carrying information.

question: What is another term for the mixing of two RF signals?
optionC: Frequency inversion
explanation: Heterodyning is mixing two RF signals in a nonlinear device to produce sum and difference frequencies. Synthesizing means generating a frequency, not combining two signals.

question: Which of the following describes Baudot code?
optionA: A 7-bit code with start, stop, and parity bits
optionB: A code using error detection and correction
optionC: A 5-bit code with additional start and stop bits
optionD: A code using SELCAL and LISTEN
explanation: Baudot (ITA2) is a 5-bit code used for RTTY, with start and stop bits added to each character. The 7-bit code with parity is ASCII.

question: What emission is produced by a reactance modulator connected to a transmitter RF amplifier stage?
optionC: Amplitude modulation
explanation: A reactance modulator changes the reactance seen by an amplifier stage, which shifts the phase of the RF passing through it, so the result is phase modulation. Used on an oscillator instead, the same circuit gives FM.

question: What is the stage in a VHF FM transmitter that generates a harmonic of a lower frequency signal to reach the desired operating frequency?
optionC: Balanced converter
explanation: A frequency multiplier makes a harmonic of a lower-frequency oscillator, for example a 12.21 MHz stage multiplied by 12 to reach 146.52 MHz. A mixer would add or subtract two frequencies instead.

question: In an ARQ mode, what is meant by a NAK response to a transmitted packet?
optionC: Receiving station connected and ready for transmissions
explanation: NAK means negative acknowledgment: the packet arrived with errors, so the receiving station asks for it to be sent again. An ACK would mean it was received without error.

question: What type of modulation varies the instantaneous power level of the RF signal?
optionC: Frequency modulation
explanation: Amplitude modulation varies the RF amplitude, and so its instantaneous power, with the modulating signal. FM and phase modulation keep the amplitude constant.

question: Which intermodulation products are closest to the original signal frequencies?
optionC: Odd-order
explanation: Odd-order products such as 2F1 - F2 and 2F2 - F1 fall close to the original frequencies, often inside the passband, which makes them the troublesome ones. Even-order products land far away and are easy to filter.

question: What action results from a failure to exchange information due to excessive transmission attempts when using an ARQ mode?
optionC: Packets will be routed incorrectly
optionD: Encoding reverts to the default character set
explanation: When too many retries fail, an ARQ link gives up and the connection is dropped. The protocol does not change character sets or reroute packets because of it.

question: Which of the following is characteristic of QPSK31?
optionC: Its bandwidth is approximately the same as BPSK31
explanation: All listed items are true of QPSK31: its four phase states make it sideband sensitive, its convolutional encoding gives error correction, and it fits in roughly the same 31 Hz bandwidth as BPSK31.

question: What is the total bandwidth of an FM phone transmission having 5 kHz deviation and 3 kHz modulating frequency?
optionC: 8 kHz
explanation: By Carson's rule, bandwidth = 2 x (deviation + highest modulating frequency) = 2 x (5 kHz + 3 kHz) = 16 kHz. Adding 5 and 3 to get 8 kHz forgets the factor of two for both sidebands.

question: Which of the following narrow-band digital modes can receive signals with very low signal-to-noise ratios?
optionC: AMTOR
explanation: FT8 can decode signals down to about -20 dB signal-to-noise ratio in a 2.5 kHz bandwidth, well below what a human ear can copy. MSK144 is for short meteor scatter bursts, not continuous weak signals.

question: Which of the following phone emissions uses the narrowest bandwidth?
optionC: Phase modulation
explanation: Single sideband sends only one sideband with no carrier, so it needs about 2.4 to 3 kHz, the least of these phone emissions. FM and phase modulation phone use far more, about 10 to 16 kHz.

question: What is the frequency deviation for a 12.21 MHz reactance modulated oscillator in a 5 kHz deviation, 146.52 MHz FM phone transmitter?
optionC: 5 kHz
explanation: The multiplication factor is 146.52 / 12.21 = 12, so the oscillator needs only 5,000 Hz / 12 = 416.7 Hz of deviation to produce 5 kHz at the output frequency.

question: Which of the following statements is true about PSK31?
optionA: Upper case letters are sent with more power
optionB: Upper case letters use longer Varicode bit sequences and thus slow down transmission
optionC: Error correction is used to ensure accurate message reception
optionD: Higher power is needed as compared to RTTY for similar error rates
explanation: PSK31 uses Varicode, which gives common lower case letters short codes and upper case letters longer ones, so typing in capitals slows the transmission. PSK31 has no error correction and needs less power than RTTY.

question: Which of the following is an effect of overmodulation?
optionC: Frequency drift
explanation: Overmodulation distorts the signal and generates splatter, spreading energy far outside the normal channel, so the main effect is excessive bandwidth that can interfere with nearby stations.

question: Why is it important to know the duty cycle of the mode you are using when transmitting?
optionA: To aid in tuning your transmitter
optionB: Some modes have high duty cycles that could exceed the transmitter’s average power rating
optionC: To allow time for the other station to break in during a transmission
explanation: Modes such as FM, RTTY and many digital modes transmit at full power almost continuously, so their average power is close to peak and can exceed the transmitter's average power rating. You may need to reduce power for them.

question: Which is true of mesh network microwave nodes?
optionA: Having more nodes increases signal strengths
optionB: If one node fails, a packet may still reach its target station via an alternate node
optionC: Links between two nodes in a network may have different frequencies and bandwidths
optionD: More nodes reduce overall microwave out of band interference
explanation: A mesh network routes data through whichever nodes are available, so if one node fails, a packet can still reach its destination through another path. More nodes do not raise signal strength.

question: What type of modulation is used by FT8?
optionC: Amplitude compressed AM
explanation: FT8 sends its symbols as 8-tone frequency shift keying, using eight tones spaced 6.25 Hz apart for a total bandwidth of about 50 Hz.

question: Why is it good to match receiver bandwidth to the bandwidth of the operating mode?
optionA: It is required by FCC rules
optionB: It minimizes power consumption in the receiver
optionC: It improves impedance matching of the antenna
optionD: It results in the best signal-to-noise ratio
explanation: A receive bandwidth matched to the signal lets in all of the signal but as little noise as possible, giving the best signal-to-noise ratio. FCC rules do not set receiver bandwidths.

question: How does forward error correction (FEC) allow the receiver to correct data errors?
optionA: By controlling transmitter output power for optimum signal strength
optionB: By using the Varicode character set
optionC: By transmitting redundant information with the data
optionD: By using a parity bit with each character
explanation: FEC sends redundant information along with the data, so the receiver can rebuild missing or damaged bits without asking for a repeat. A single parity bit can only detect some errors, not fix them.

question: What is meant by the term “flat-topping,” when referring to an amplitude-modulated phone signal?
optionA: Signal distortion caused by insufficient collector current
optionB: The transmitter’s automatic level control (ALC) is properly adjusted
optionC: Signal distortion caused by excessive drive or speech levels
optionD: The transmitter’s carrier is properly suppressed
explanation: Flat-topping is distortion when too much drive or microphone gain pushes the amplifier past its peak output, clipping the top of the envelope. That clipping makes splatter and a wider signal.

question: What is the relationship between transmitted symbol rate and bandwidth?
optionA: Symbol rate and bandwidth are not related
optionB: Higher symbol rates require wider bandwidth
optionC: Lower symbol rates require wider bandwidth
optionD: Bandwidth is half the symbol rate
explanation: Sending more symbols per second needs a wider bandwidth; the occupied bandwidth rises roughly in proportion to the symbol rate. Lower symbol rates allow narrower signals, which is why weak-signal modes are slow.

question: How are the two separate frequencies of a Frequency Shift Keyed (FSK) signal identified?
optionC: High and low
explanation: The two FSK frequencies are called mark and space, terms carried over from telegraph and teletype practice. Dot and dash describe Morse code.

question: What is the modulation envelope of an AM signal?
optionA: The waveform created by connecting the peak values of the modulated signal
optionB: The carrier frequency that contains the signal
optionC: Spurious signals that envelop nearby frequencies
optionD: The bandwidth of the modulated signal
explanation: The modulation envelope is the outline formed by joining the peaks of the modulated RF wave; in AM it follows the shape of the audio. It is not the carrier or the bandwidth.

question: What combination of a mixer’s Local Oscillator (LO) and RF input frequencies is found in the output?
optionC: The sum and difference
explanation: A mixer's output contains the sum and difference of the LO and RF frequencies, for example 14.2 MHz and 9 MHz give 23.2 MHz and 5.2 MHz. Filters then pick the one used as the IF.

question: Which type of code is used for sending characters in a PSK31 signal?
optionC: Volumetric
explanation: PSK31 sends characters in Varicode, a variable-length code in which common characters have the shortest bit patterns. Viterbi is a decoding method, not the character code.

question: What is QPSK modulation?
optionA: Modulation using quasi-parallel to serial conversion to reduce bandwidth
optionB: Modulation using quadra-pole sideband keying to generate spread spectrum signals
optionC: Modulation using Fast Fourier Transforms to generate frequencies at the first, second, third, and fourth harmonics of the carrier frequency to improve noise immunity
optionD: Modulation in which digital data is transmitted using 0-, 90-, 180- and 270-degrees phase shift to represent pairs of bits
explanation: QPSK uses four carrier phases, 0, 90, 180 and 270 degrees, each standing for a pair of bits, so it carries two bits per symbol.

question: What process combines two signals in a non-linear circuit to produce unwanted spurious outputs?
optionC: Detection
explanation: Intermodulation is the unwanted mixing of two or more signals in a nonlinear circuit, producing spurious outputs at combinations of their frequencies. Heterodyning is the same mixing done on purpose.

question: What is indicated on a waterfall display by one or more vertical lines on either side of a data mode or RTTY signal?
optionC: Insufficient modulation
explanation: Vertical lines on either side of a data or RTTY trace on a waterfall show spurious sidebands from overmodulation, often from too much audio drive. Lower the audio level until they disappear.

question: What is a link budget?
optionA: The financial costs associated with operating a radio link
optionB: The sum of antenna gains minus system losses
optionC: The sum of transmit power and antenna gains minus system losses as seen at the receiver
optionD: The difference between transmit power and receiver sensitivity
explanation: A link budget adds transmit power and antenna gains, then subtracts losses such as feed line and path loss, to get the signal level seen at the receiver. The sum of gains minus losses alone leaves out transmit power.

question: Which of the following is an odd-order intermodulation product of frequencies F1 and F2?
explanation: The order of a product is the sum of the multipliers, so 2F1 - F2 is 2 + 1 = 3, an odd-order product. 5F1 - 3F2 is 8th order and 3F1 - F2 is 4th order, both even, so not every listed product is odd-order.

question: Which of the following describes a waterfall display?
optionA: Frequency is horizontal, signal strength is vertical, time is intensity
optionB: Frequency is vertical, signal strength is intensity, time is horizontal
optionC: Frequency is horizontal, signal strength is intensity, time is vertical
optionD: Frequency is vertical, signal strength is horizontal, time is intensity
explanation: On a waterfall, frequency runs across the screen horizontally, signal strength is shown by brightness or color, and time scrolls down the screen vertically.

question: What is link margin?
optionB: The difference between received power level and minimum required signal level at the input to the receiver
optionC: Transmit power minus receiver sensitivity
explanation: Link margin is how far the received power is above the minimum level the receiver needs. For example, a -90 dBm signal into a receiver that needs -110 dBm gives a 20 dB margin.

question: What does an FT8 signal report of +3 mean?
optionA: The signal is 3 times the noise level of an equivalent SSB signal
optionC: The signal-to-noise ratio is equivalent to +3dB in a 2.5 kHz bandwidth
optionD: The signal is 3 dB over S9
explanation: FT8 reports are signal-to-noise ratio in dB referenced to a 2.5 kHz bandwidth, so +3 means the signal is 3 dB above the noise in that bandwidth. It is not an S-meter reading.

question: Which of the following provide digital voice modes?
optionC: Winlink, PACTOR II, and PACTOR III
explanation: DMR, D-STAR and System Fusion are digital voice modes. FT8, FT4 and FST4 are weak-signal data modes, and Winlink and PACTOR carry text and email.

question: Which of the following factors determine the characteristic impedance of a parallel conductor feed line?
optionA: The distance between the centers of the conductors and the radius of the conductors
optionB: The distance between the centers of the conductors and the length of the line
optionC: The radius of the conductors and the frequency of the signal
optionD: The frequency of the signal and the length of the line
explanation: The characteristic impedance of a parallel conductor line depends on its geometry: the spacing between the conductor centers and the conductor radius. It does not depend on line length or frequency.

question: What is a characteristic of a random-wire HF antenna connected directly to the transmitter?
optionA: It must be longer than 1 wavelength
optionB: Station equipment may carry significant RF current
optionC: It produces only vertically polarized radiation
optionD: It is more effective on the lower HF bands than on the higher bands
explanation: A random wire fed directly from the transmitter uses the station as part of the antenna system, so the rig and other equipment may carry significant RF current. That can cause RF burns and interference in the shack.

question: Which of the following would increase the bandwidth of a Yagi antenna?
optionC: Loading coils in series with the element
explanation: Larger-diameter elements have a lower Q, which widens a Yagi's usable bandwidth. Loading coils do the opposite and narrow it.

question: Which of the following antenna types will be most effective as a near vertical incidence skywave (NVIS) antenna for short-skip communications on 40 meters during the day?
optionA: A horizontal dipole placed between 1/10 and 1/4 wavelength above the ground
optionB: A vertical antenna placed between 1/4 and 1/2 wavelength above the ground
optionC: A horizontal dipole placed at approximately 1/2 wavelength above the ground
optionD: A vertical dipole placed at approximately 1/2 wavelength above the ground
explanation: A horizontal dipole only 1/10 to 1/4 wavelength high sends most energy nearly straight up, which the ionosphere reflects back down nearby, ideal for 40 m NVIS by day. Verticals put little energy at high angles.

question: What is the relationship between high standing wave ratio (SWR) and transmission line loss?
optionA: There is no relationship between transmission line loss and SWR
optionB: High SWR increases loss in a lossy transmission line
optionC: High SWR makes it difficult to measure transmission line loss
optionD: High SWR reduces the relative effect of transmission line loss
explanation: High SWR means more power travels back and forth on the line, so more is lost to heat in a lossy line. On a low-loss line the extra loss from moderate SWR can be small.

question: Which of the following is a common way to adjust the feed point impedance of an elevated quarter-wave ground-plane vertical antenna to be approximately 50 ohms?
optionC: Lengthen the radials beyond one wavelength
explanation: Sloping the radials of an elevated quarter-wave ground plane downward raises the feed point impedance from about 36 ohms toward 50 ohms, giving a better match to coax.

question: What is the approximate length of the driven element of a Yagi antenna?
optionC: 3/4 wavelength
explanation: The driven element of a Yagi is roughly a half-wave dipole, about 1/2 wavelength long. The parasitic elements are cut a little longer or shorter than that.

question: What is the feed point impedance of an end-fed half-wave antenna?
optionC: Approximately 300 ohms
explanation: An end-fed half-wave antenna is fed at a voltage maximum where current is low, so its feed point impedance is very high, typically a few thousand ohms. A matching transformer is used.

question: What is the nominal characteristic impedance of “window line” transmission line?
optionC: 100 ohms
explanation: Window line, the ladder-style twin lead with slots in the insulation, has a nominal characteristic impedance of about 450 ohms. 50 and 75 ohms are typical coax impedances.

question: Which of the following best describes the radiation pattern of a quarter-wave ground-plane vertical antenna?
optionC: Hemispherical
explanation: A quarter-wave ground-plane vertical radiates equally in all compass directions, so it is omnidirectional in azimuth. It is not isotropic because it puts little energy straight up.

question: How do the lengths of a three-element Yagi reflector and director compare to that of the driven element?
optionA: The reflector is longer, and the director is shorter
optionB: The reflector is shorter, and the director is longer
optionC: They are all the same length
optionD: Relative length depends on the frequency of operation
explanation: In a three-element Yagi the reflector is a little longer than the driven element and the director a little shorter. That arrangement makes the beam fire toward the director.

question: In which direction is the maximum radiation from a VHF/UHF “halo” antenna?
optionA: Broadside to the plane of the halo
optionC: Omnidirectional in the plane of the halo
optionD: On the same side as the feed point
explanation: A halo is a horizontal loop-like dipole bent into a circle, so it radiates fairly evenly in all directions in the plane of the halo, giving horizontally polarized omnidirectional coverage.

question: What causes reflected power at an antenna’s feed point?
optionA: Operating an antenna at its resonant frequency
optionB: Using more transmitter power than the antenna can handle
optionC: A difference between feed line impedance and antenna feed point impedance
optionD: Feeding the antenna with unbalanced feed line
explanation: Power is reflected at the feed point when the antenna's feed point impedance differs from the feed line's characteristic impedance. Running an antenna at resonance does not by itself cause reflections.

question: What is the radiation pattern of a dipole antenna in free space in a plane containing the conductor?
optionA: It is a figure-eight at right angles to the antenna
optionB: It is a figure-eight off both ends of the antenna
optionC: It is a circle (equal radiation in all directions)
optionD: It has a pair of lobes on one side of the antenna and a single lobe on the other side
explanation: A dipole in free space radiates most broadside to the wire and almost nothing off its ends, giving a figure-eight pattern at right angles to the antenna. The nulls are off the ends.

question: How does antenna gain in dBi compare to gain stated in dBd for the same antenna?
optionA: Gain in dBi is 2.15 dB lower
optionB: Gain in dBi is 2.15 dB higher
optionC: Gain in dBd is 1.25 dBd lower
optionD: Gain in dBd is 1.25 dBd higher
explanation: dBi compares gain to an isotropic radiator and dBd to a dipole, which already has 2.15 dBi of gain, so gain in dBi is 2.15 dB higher. A 7 dBd beam is about 9.15 dBi.

question: What is the primary function of antenna traps?
optionC: To provide balanced feed point impedance
explanation: Traps are parallel tuned circuits that act as switches, cutting off part of the antenna on higher bands so one antenna can work on several bands. They are not filters for spurious signals.

question: How does the attenuation of coaxial cable change with increasing frequency?
optionC: Attenuation decreases
optionD: Attenuation follows Marconi’s Law of Attenuation
explanation: Coax loss increases as frequency goes up, mainly because of skin effect in the conductors and dielectric loss. That is why a run of RG-58 that is fine on 80 m can be very lossy at UHF.

question: How does antenna height affect the azimuthal radiation pattern of a horizontal dipole HF antenna at elevation angles higher than about 45 degrees?
optionA: If the antenna is too high, the pattern becomes unpredictable
optionB: Antenna height has no effect on the pattern
optionC: If the antenna is less than 1/2 wavelength high, the azimuthal pattern is almost omnidirectional
optionD: If the antenna is less than 1/2 wavelength high, radiation off the ends of the wire is eliminated
explanation: Below about 1/2 wavelength, ground reflections push most of the dipole's radiation upward, so at high elevation angles its azimuthal pattern is almost omnidirectional. This is the basis of NVIS operation.

question: What is the primary effect of increasing boom length and adding directors to a Yagi antenna?
optionC: Front-to-back ratio decreases
explanation: A longer boom with more directors concentrates more energy in the forward direction, so gain increases and the beam gets narrower, not wider.

question: What is an advantage of vertically stacking horizontally polarized Yagi antennas?
optionA: It allows quick selection of vertical or horizontal polarization
optionB: It allows simultaneous vertical and horizontal polarization
optionC: It narrows the main lobe in azimuth
optionD: It narrows the main lobe in elevation
explanation: Stacking horizontal Yagis vertically narrows the main lobe in elevation, putting more energy at low angles and adding gain. Azimuth beamwidth is set by each Yagi and stays about the same.

question: In what units is RF feed line loss usually expressed?
optionC: Ohms per 100 feet
explanation: Feed line loss is usually listed in decibels per 100 feet at a stated frequency. Ohms describe impedance, not loss.

question: Where should the radial wires of a ground-mounted vertical antenna system be placed?
optionA: As high as possible above the ground
optionC: On the surface or buried a few inches below the ground
optionD: At the center of the antenna
explanation: Radials for a ground-mounted vertical are laid on the ground surface or buried a few inches deep, spreading out from the base. Raising them high makes it an elevated ground plane instead.

question: What does “front-to-back ratio” mean in reference to a Yagi antenna?
optionA: The number of directors versus the number of reflectors
optionB: The relative position of the driven element with respect to the reflectors and directors
optionC: The power radiated in the major lobe compared to that in the opposite direction
optionD: The ratio of forward gain to dipole gain
explanation: Front-to-back ratio compares the power radiated in the main lobe with the power radiated in the opposite direction, usually given in dB. A higher ratio means better rejection off the back.

question: Which of the following is an advantage of a log-periodic antenna?
optionB: Higher gain per element than a Yagi antenna
optionC: Harmonic suppression
explanation: A log-periodic antenna works over a wide frequency range, often covering several bands with good SWR. It gives less gain per element than a Yagi.

question: What must be done to prevent standing waves on a feed line connected to an antenna?
optionA: The antenna feed point must be at DC ground potential
optionB: The feed line must be an odd number of electrical quarter wavelengths long
optionC: The feed line must be an even number of physical half wavelengths long
optionD: The antenna feed point impedance must be matched to the characteristic impedance of the feed line
explanation: Standing waves disappear only when the load impedance equals the line's characteristic impedance. Choosing a special line length does not stop reflections; it only changes what impedance is seen at the far end.

question: How does the feed point impedance of a horizontal 1/2 wave dipole antenna change as the antenna height is reduced to 1/10 wavelength above ground?
optionC: It peaks at about 1/8 wavelength above ground
optionD: It is unaffected by the height above ground
explanation: As a horizontal dipole is lowered toward the ground, coupling to the ground lowers its feed point impedance steadily below the free-space value of about 72 ohms. At 1/10 wavelength it is well under 50 ohms.

question: What is meant by the “main lobe” of a directive antenna?
optionA: The magnitude of the maximum vertical angle of radiation
optionB: The point of maximum current in a radiating antenna element
optionC: The maximum voltage standing wave point on a radiating element
optionD: The direction of maximum radiated field strength from the antenna
explanation: The main lobe is the direction in which a directive antenna radiates its strongest field. It is not about current or voltage points along an element.

question: Which of the following describes a log-periodic antenna?
optionA: Element length and spacing vary logarithmically along the boom
optionB: Impedance varies periodically as a function of frequency
optionC: Gain varies logarithmically as a function of frequency
optionD: SWR varies periodically as a function of boom length
explanation: In a log-periodic antenna the element lengths and spacings change by a constant ratio along the boom, a logarithmic progression that makes its properties repeat with frequency.

question: If the SWR on an antenna feed line is 5:1, and a matching network at the transmitter end of the feed line is adjusted to present a 1:1 SWR to the transmitter, what is the resulting SWR on the feed line?
optionC: Between 1:1 and 5:1 depending on the characteristic impedance of the line
optionD: Between 1:1 and 5:1 depending on the reflected power at the transmitter
explanation: A matching network at the transmitter only changes what the transmitter sees; the mismatch at the antenna still sets the SWR on the line, so it stays 5:1. The line SWR could only drop if the match were made at the antenna.

question: How does the feed point impedance of a 1/2 wave dipole change as the feed point is moved from the center toward the ends?
optionC: It peaks at about 1/8 wavelength from the end
optionD: It is unaffected by the location of the feed point
explanation: Toward the ends of a half-wave dipole the current falls and the voltage rises, so the feed point impedance increases steadily from about 72 ohms at the center to a few thousand ohms at the ends.

question: In free space, how does the gain of two three-element, horizontally polarized Yagi antennas spaced vertically 1/2 wavelength apart typically compare to the gain of a single three-element Yagi?
optionC: Approximately 6 dB higher
